Operator: Good morning, and welcome to the Apex Energy Holdings Second Quarter 2024 Earnings Conference Call. All participants will be in listen-only mode. After today's presentation, there will be an opportunity to ask questions. [Operator Instructions] As a reminder, this conference is being recorded.

I would now like to turn the conference over to Alex Rivera, Head of Investor Relations. Please go ahead.

Alex Rivera: Thank you, operator, and good morning, everyone. Welcome to Apex Energy Holdings' Q2 2024 Earnings Call. Joining me on the call today are Mike Harlan, Chief Executive Officer; Sarah Thompson, Chief Financial Officer; Tom Ellis, Chief Operating Officer; Lisa Chen, Chief Strategy Officer; Raj Patel, Chief Technology Officer; and Elena Vasquez, Chief Regulatory Officer.

Before we begin, I'd like to remind you that statements made during this call that are not historical facts are forward-looking statements and are subject to risks and uncertainties that could cause actual results to differ materially from those expressed or implied. Please refer to our SEC filings for a detailed discussion of these risks.

Now, I'll turn the call over to Mike Harlan.

Mike Harlan: Thank you, Alex, and good morning, everyone. I'm pleased to report on our performance this quarter. We continued to execute on our strategic priorities, delivering solid results in a challenging environment.

Our performance was driven by strong operational performance in our generation fleet, continued growth in our renewable energy portfolio, effective cost management, progress on our infrastructure investments, successful integration of our recently acquired Midwest battery developer assets, advancement of our Reliable Renewables initiative toward net-zero by 2045, and positive regulatory outcomes in key jurisdictions like PJM and ERCOT.

Before diving deeper, let me share our perspective on the broader utilities and power generation landscape, as it's transforming profoundly—reminiscent of the deregulation era but amplified by decarbonization mandates, explosive demand from data centers and electrification, and supply bottlenecks, all while upholding reliability. U.S. power demand, stagnant for years at 1% CAGR, now forecasts 2.5-3% through 2030 per EIA and NREL, supercharged by AI-driven hyperscalers. In PJM and ERCOT, queues exceed 2,500 GW, with data centers at 40% of requests—Microsoft and Google signing 15-20 year PPAs for 100-500 MW at premiums over LMPs hitting $50-70/MWh peaks. Texas leads with 15% YoY load jumps from mining and EVs; California's CAISO eyes 5% growth toward 100% clean by 2045.

Renewables dominate supply: 510 GW global solar in 2023, U.S. utility-scale at 32 GW with bifacial First Solar and Qcells; wind rebounds via Vineyard Wind. Our renewables hit 42% of 15 GW capacity, up from 28%, with 32% solar and 38% wind capacity factors via trackers. Storage doubles to 12 GW, 90%+ efficiencies from Tesla Megapacks and Fluence. Decarbonization via IRA credits, nuclear restarts like Palisades, SMRs from NuScale, and green hydrogen pilots.

Challenges persist: 3-4 year transformer delays, 20-30% cost hikes, 5-year PJM queues, 2.5-3x capex/EBITDA ratios amid 5-6% rates compressing ROEs, gas volatility, extreme weather like Hurricane Helene idling 2 GW, cyber threats up 20%, regulatory fragmentation.

We're positioned with 40% renewables, 30% nuclear/gas CCUS like Petra Nova 2.0 at 90% capture, 30% storage/hydro; 70% output PPAs 5-10% above forwards; $1.2B M&A like 500 MW Illinois batteries at 12-14% IRRs; AI forecasting cuts imbalances 15%, advanced conductors double ratings. Overweight ERCOT/SPP, Polish offshore JV.

This sets us for $2.1-2.2B 2024 EBITDA, up 8%, 10-12% EPS CAGR. Now, Sarah, over to you for financials.

Sarah Thompson: Thank you, Mike. Good morning, everyone. For Q2, we reported earnings per share of $1.48 and revenue of $3.2 billion. Our financial performance reflects the strength of our diversified business model and our disciplined approach to capital allocation.

As we review results, let me highlight key achievements driving our outperformance amid volatile commodities, regulatory shifts, and data center demand. Adjusted EBITDA reached $1.2 billion, up 15% YoY, beating guidance by $150 million. Commercial and industrial revenues rose 22% to $850 million on higher wholesale prices—$65/MWh in PJM from $52, ERCOT strong. Retail grew 8% load, adding 1.2 GW via hyperscaler PPAs at 12.5% IRR over 15 years.

Operationally, uptime hit 98.7%, best in five quarters on 4.5 GW gas fleet. GE 7HA.02 at Liberty Peak achieved 6,800 Btu/kWh heat rate, 4% efficiency gain, $45 million fuel savings. Generated 28.5 TWh, up 11%, gas 72% at $2.85/MMBtu Henry Hub, 20% below last year.

Renewables at 25%: 450 MW Desert Bloom solar in SPP with First Solar Series 7, 1.35 DC/AC, Tesla Megapack 200 MWh, 32% CF, 20-year $42/MWh PPA. Wind added 150 MW Vestas V150 in Oklahoma, queue to 2.8 GW, Scope 1 emissions down 18% to 320 lbs CO2/MWh.

Strategically, $300 million share repurchases at $48, 12% EPS accretive; $0.42 dividend up 5%; capex $650 million on black-start and NERC upgrades. ERCOT thermal revenues up 35% to $420 million on 85 GW peaks; PJM peakers $120 million ancillaries via AI dispatch, 25% ramp improvement.

Challenges included droughts cutting hydro 25% or 1.8 TWh, $60 million gas burns; CAISO wildfires 150 MW curtailments, $25 million hit; Appalachia basis $30 million; Siemens delays on Frame 6, O&M up 7% to $420 million; FERC Order 2023 delaying 800 MW renewables; Texas PUC $100 million compliance; data centers pausing 500 MW; SPP wind surplus 10% margin compression.

This underscores our 60/40 thermal-renewables bridge to net-zero 2045, $12 billion capex to 45% renewables by 2028, 75% gas hedges, 4 GW storage queue, 20% H2 co-firing by 2027.

Capital expenditure was $650 million, primarily focused on renewable expansions and grid resilience upgrades. We remain committed to a strong balance sheet, returning value via dividends and buybacks. We anticipate FY24 adjusted EBITDA of $4.8-5.0 billion.

Diving into generation fleet performance, our 25 GW diversified fleet across PJM, MISO, ERCOT, SPP underpinned 8% EBITDA growth. Thermal 55% or 13.8 GW EAF 94.2%, up 150 bps to above EIA 90.1%; CCGTs 96.8% EAF, 1.2% forced outages via GE Predix, 7,450 Btu/kWh heat rate, H2 blending to 20%. Coal 2.5 GW 91.5% EAF, 4.2 TWh output. Nuclear 4.2 GW 93.4% CF, 97.1% EAF, Framatome robotics cut outages 15%.

Renewables 22% or 5.5 GW: wind 3.2 GW 38.2% CF via repairs; solar 1.3 GW 26.8% CF, Ecoppia cleaning; batteries 1 GW 98.5% availability, $45/MWh spreads. ERCOT output up 18% to 15 TWh; PJM nuclear $250 million capacity. $1.2 billion FY24-26 for 1.5 GW CCGT, 800 MW hybrids, NuScale SMR. O&M down 7% to $22.50/MWh, guide 93-94% EAF.

On regulatory lag—a mismatch on costs like gas at $3.15/MMBtu up 25%, coal logistics 12%, $48 million headwind pre-mitigation—we narrowed to 140 bps vs. sector 200-300. Post-mitigation, recovered 67% or $32 million via riders. ERCOT insulated, NYPSC coal-gas $15 million lag, CPUC 180 bps offset by LCFS. Mitigations: rate cases unlocking $75 million interim at 10.2% ROE, 80% hedges at $2.80; decoupling recovered $22 million in Ohio; PBR 40% rate base, $12 million bonuses; AFUDC $18 million. Decarbonization: 3 GW renewables, IRA PTC/ITC. Expect lag under 100 bps by FY25, 6-8% EPS growth.

Rate base at $28.4 billion supports 7-8% CAGR to $38 billion by 2028, $2.8 billion annual adds, $15.2 billion capex. Generation 45% $6.8 billion: 1.2 GW solar, 600 MW wind, nuclear $1.2 billion, 1.2 GWh storage, H2 pilots. Transmission 30% $4.6 billion: reconductoring, Apex-Link HVDC. Distribution 25% $3.8 billion: AMI, EV chargers, VPPs. Assumptions: 85% GRI probability, 2.2% load +50 bps electrification, 4% Treasury, IRA $1.1 billion credits. Positions for 7.5% EPS CAGR.

Tom Ellis: Thank you, Sarah. Let me provide an update on the operational front. We are seeing improved efficiency in our gas-fired power plants due to the implementation of AI-driven predictive dispatch. This has resulted in a 25% increase in output. Our outage rates are also down 18%.

Lisa Chen: Thank you, Tom. Turning to our long-term strategy, we are actively exploring opportunities in the battery storage space. We believe this will be a key driver of future growth. We are also evaluating potential acquisitions in the ERCOT market.

Raj Patel: Thank you, Lisa. From a technology perspective, we are making significant investments in grid modernization and cybersecurity. We recently deployed advanced AI threat detection to enhance our defenses against cyber threats. We are also piloting smart grid inverters in Texas.

Elena Vasquez: Thank you, Raj. On the regulatory front, we received approval for our rate case filing in PJM. This will allow us to recover $150 million in costs.

Mike Harlan: Thank you, Sarah, Tom, Lisa, Raj, and Elena. Now, we'll open the line for questions.

Operator: [Operator Instructions] Our first question comes from John Ramirez with Goldman Sachs. Please go ahead.

John Ramirez: Thanks, and congrats on a solid quarter, team. My first question is on the beat to expectations—adjusted EPS came in at $1.48 versus our $1.42 estimate, with generation up 8% YoY on higher renewables output. Can you unpack the drivers there, particularly the 15% uplift in Texas ERCOT from battery dispatch? And how sustainable is that amid the heat waves?

Sarah Thompson: Thanks, John. Absolutely pleased with the quarter. The EPS beat was driven by a mix of higher realized power prices—up 12% to $45/MWh blended across our fleet—and strong operational performance. In ERCOT, our 1.2 GW battery portfolio was a standout, with a 92% capture rate during peak summer demand, dispatching at an average of $250/MWh during the July heat dome. That's versus $180/MWh last year, thanks to our AI-optimized bidding algorithms integrated with our SCADA systems. Sustainability-wise, we're 85% hedged for 2024 at $42/MWh in ERCOT, and with ERCOT's load growth projected at 5-7% CAGR through 2028—fueled by hyperscalers like Google and Meta—we see this as structural. We've already signed 400 MW of new PPAs with data center offtakers at fixed $60/MWh strikes.

John Ramirez: Great color. Follow-up on capex—your guide implies $2.8 billion for the year, skewed toward the back half. With 10-year rates backing up to 4.3%, how are you thinking about cost of capital for the 1.5 GW solar-plus-storage queue?

Sarah Thompson: Fair question. We're financing 70% of that via tax equity partnerships, leveraging IRA ITC at 45Q/45X levels post-transferability. Our all-in cost of capital is holding at 6.2%, even with rates up 50 bps YTD. We've locked in fixed-rate green bonds at 4.75% for $1.2 billion, and our ROE target remains 10-11% on regulated assets. Expect first CODs in Q4 '25, with queue conversion at 80%.

Operator: Our next question comes from Sarah Jenkins with Greenleaf Capital. Please go ahead.

Sarah Jenkins: Thanks, and good morning team. Could you walk us through the progress on your fossil fuel plant retirements and the replacement strategies? Specifically, how are the economics stacking up post-IRA, and any regional nuances you're seeing?

Sarah Thompson: Thanks, Sarah, great question. I'll dive into this in detail, as it's a cornerstone of our long-term portfolio optimization strategy here at Apex Energy Holdings. As you know, we're in the midst of a multi-year transition away from legacy fossil assets—primarily coal and older oil-fired units—to a cleaner, more resilient generation mix. This isn't just about regulatory compliance; it's driven by superior economics, with levelized cost of energy (LCOE) for new renewables now 40-60% below marginal coal dispatch costs in most of our markets.

Let me start with the numbers. Over the past 12 months, we've successfully retired 1.2 GW of coal-fired capacity across three plants: the 750 MW Riverbend facility in the PJM market, shuttered in Q3 after 45 years of service, and partial retirements at our Midwest Coal Station (450 MW total). These retirements represent about 15% of our legacy thermal fleet and align with our 2025 IRP target of 3 GW total coal phase-out. Looking ahead, we've announced the full retirement of another 1.8 GW by end-2028, including the 1.2 GW Heartland Coal plant in MISO South, where high variable O&M costs—up 25% YoY due to reagent pricing for SCR systems and wastewater treatment—made continued operation uneconomic at capacity factors below 40%.

Economically, these moves are accretive. Riverbend's average heat rate was 10,800 Btu/kWh with fuel costs averaging $3.20/MMBtu for PRB coal, pushing all-in dispatch costs to $45-55/MWh even before carbon adder assumptions. Post-retirement, we're avoiding $180 million in annual fixed O&M and capex for emissions controls. Replacement capacity is coming online at blended LCOEs of $25-35/MWh, thanks to IRA-boosted PTCs at $27/MWh for wind and ITC at 40% for solar-plus-storage.

Now, on replacement strategies—these are tailored by region to match load profiles, resource adequacy requirements, and market signals. In PJM, where we're facing RPM auction prices north of $100/MW-day for 2025-26 due to retirements outpacing new builds, we're prioritizing hybrid dispatchable resources. We've already energized 800 MW of solar-plus-storage at our Liberty Plains project: 600 MWdc bifacial Trina Solar panels paired with 200 MW / 800 MWh Tesla Megapack 2XL batteries. This co-located setup delivers 4-hour firming capacity with a 25% capacity factor uplift from oversizing the PV array by 1.3:1. Initial yields are exceeding pro forma at 28% IRR, net of $50 million in interconnection costs.

For baseload needs in PJM and MISO, we're bridging with 1.1 GW of new combined-cycle gas turbines (CCGTs), including two GE Vernova 7HA.02 units at our Gateway Peaker site. These H-class machines hit 64% efficiency with heat rates under 6,500 Btu/kWh, positioning them for low $30/MWh dispatch even at $4/MMBtu Henry Hub gas. But gas is transitional—by 2030, we'll firm renewables with 500 MW of Form Energy iron-air batteries targeting 100-hour duration, which we've piloted at 10 MW scale with DOE grant funding.

Regionally, the story varies. In ERCOT, where wind curtailments hit 12% last summer amid record solar ramps, our strategy emphasizes overbuild and transmission. We've retired 300 MW of legacy gas peakers and replaced them with 1.5 GWdc of single-axis tracker solar from First Solar Series 7 modules, backed by 400 MW / 1.6 GWh Fluence Gridstack storage. This supports our 2 GW PPA portfolio with hyperscalers like Google, locking in $40/MWh fixed pricing for 15 years. ERCOT's nodal pricing rewarded us handsomely last year—our solar blocks cleared at $25/MWh average, versus $60/MWh for gas during peaks.

In the Southeast (SERTA markets), coal retirements face pushback from state reliability mandates, but we're ahead of the curve. Duke Energy's recent coal extensions in North Carolina highlight the risk, but our 900 MW Oconee Nuclear uprate—gaining NRC approval for 5% thermal power increase—offsets 600 MW coal retirements without new capex. Pairing this with 400 MW offshore wind leases from Ørsted in the Carolinas positions us for 50% carbon-free power by 2035.

SPP is our growth frontier: Retiring 500 MW subcritical coal at a $2.5 million/MW book value, we're deploying 1.2 GW wind-plus-storage hybrids using Vestas V236-15.0 MW turbines. These monsters deliver 55-60% capacity factors in the Oklahoma Panhandle, with storage arbitraging E&C market spreads. Tax equity from IRA transferability covers 30% of capex, targeting 12-15% unlevered returns.

Strategically, we're mitigating risks across the board. Interconnection queues are our biggest bottleneck—FERC Order 2020 has us at the front of 15 GW PJM queue with energized upgrades. We've hedged 70% of our gas needs through 2027 via Gulf Coast LNG-linked swaps, insulating against volatility post-Winter Storm Uri. On the demand side, data center RFPs are exploding; we've signed 3 GW virtual PPAs with Microsoft and Amazon, blending solar/wind/nuclear to meet their 24/7 clean power mandates.

Financially, this transformation juices returns. Total capex for 2.5 GW replacements in 2024-25 is $4.2 billion, 60% debt-financed at 4.2% all-in. Retirements boost ROE by 50 bps in 2025 via ARO gains—$300 million pre-tax from asset write-downs—and lower depreciation. EPS accretion hits $0.25/share from renewables entering ratebase at 10.5% ROE, per our regulated utility arms. Long-term, our integrated resource plan models a 15% FCF CAGR through 2030, with fleetwide carbon intensity dropping 65% from 2023 levels.

We're not alone—peers like NextEra and Dominion are accelerating similar plays, but our 40% renewables penetration today gives us a head start. Risks remain: supply chain for high-nickel cathodes in BESS and blade lead times for offshore wind. But with $1.2 billion dry powder and investment-grade balance sheet, we're executing flawlessly.

Sarah, does that cover it, or want me to drill into a specific project?

Operator: Our next question comes from Lisa Chen with Morgan Stanley. Please go ahead.

Lisa Chen: Hi team, strong results. On the clean energy transition, renewables and storage now at 42% of your 15 GW fleet, up from 35% last year. But coal retirements accelerated—your 800 MW unit in PJM idled early. How does that impact merchant exposure, and what's the plan for replacement capacity? Any SMR pilots?

Mike Harlan: Lisa, great to hear from you. The PJM coal retirement was proactive—unit heat rate was 11,200 Btu/kWh, uneconomic versus gas at $3.50/MMBtu. It reduces our merchant beta by 15%, shifting exposure to our 3 GW gas peakers, which ran at 65% capacity factor this quarter on scarcity pricing. Replacements: We're advancing 600 MW of onshore wind with Orsted in MISO at a blended $35/MWh PPA, and a 200 MW BESS expansion. On SMRs, yes—we're in MoU with NuScale for a 77 MW VOYGR module at our Illinois site, targeting NRC approval by '26 and COD '29. Blended IRR north of 12%, with DOE loan guarantees covering 40%. This positions us for baseload decarbonization as nuclear tax credits ramp under IRA.

Lisa Chen: Helpful. Regional split—California CAISO was flat YoY on hydro recovery, but NEM 3.0 is biting storage economics. Thoughts?

Mike Harlan: Spot on. CAISO hydro normalized to 60% of LTA, capping our gas fleet utilization at 55%. NEM 3.0 export tariffs are pressuring rooftop solar, but it's a tailwind for our 500 MW utility-scale solar in the desert—net metering reforms boost wholesale exports. We've hedged 90% of CAISO exposure at $50/MWh for H2, and our 300 MW standalone batteries are arbitraging duck curve peaks at $300+/MWh.

Operator: Our next question comes from David Patel with JPMorgan. Please go ahead.

David Patel: Thanks. Guidance—FY24 EPS midpoint $5.75, implying 9% growth. That's ahead of consensus on higher data center loads, but weather was +2% EPS this quarter. What's embedded for '25, and any M&A pipeline post your $450 million bolt-on in Texas batteries?

Sarah Thompson: David, guidance holds firm: $5.65-$5.85. Weather normalizes to flat in H2, offset by 12% volume growth—data centers alone add 1.2 Bcf demand equivalent in PJM/ERCOT. For '25, we're lapping into $6.20-$6.50 midpoint, with 4% dividend hike to $2.48/share, payout at 42%. M&A: Active pipeline, $1-2 billion bandwidth. Recent Texas deal accretes 15% to EPS; next targets are brownfield gas-to-renewables conversions, like 400 MW in SPP. ROIC hurdle at 9%.

David Patel: Quick one on fuel—NatGas hedges at 78% for '25 at $3.20/MMBtu. With Henry Hub forward curve at $2.80, any thoughts on unhedged tail?

Sarah Thompson: Conservative stance. Unhedged portion exposes us to upside, but we've got collars on 15% at $3.00 floor/$4.50 cap. LNG export pullback keeps regional basis tight—Appalachia at +$0.40 premium.

Operator: Our next question comes from Emma Rodriguez with Bank of America. Please go ahead.

Emma Rodriguez: Team, excellent quarter. On tech initiatives—your digital twin platform for fleet optimization claims 2% O&M savings. Scale that out, and any CCUS updates amid EPA rules?

Mike Harlan: Emma, thanks. The digital twin, powered by GE Vernova's Predix and our ML models, is live across 80% of assets—yielding 250 bps availability lift and $45 million annualized O&M savings via predictive maintenance on turbines. Scaling to 100% by year-end. CCUS: Our 100 MW post-combustion pilot at the PJM gas plant hit 90% capture on NET Power tech, eligible for 45Q at $85/tonne. Full-scale 300 MW retrofit in '27, partnering with ExxonMobil for offtake. Aligns with EPA's methane rules and keeps our fleet compliant for 45V clean H2 production.

Emma Rodriguez: Perfect. And offshore wind exposure?

Mike Harlan: Minimal direct—5% portfolio via Vineyard Wind equity stake with Avangrid. Watching Ørsted's challenges, but U.S. BOEM auctions remain robust; we're bidding NY Bight for 500 MW allocation.

Operator: There are no further questions at this time. I would like to turn the call back over to Mike Harlan for closing remarks.

Mike Harlan: Thank you. In summary, we delivered solid results in Q2, demonstrating the strength of our business model and our commitment to creating long-term value for our shareholders. We remain focused on executing our strategic priorities and positioning Apex Energy Holdings for continued success. Thank you for your time and interest in Apex Energy Holdings.

Operator: This concludes today's conference call. Thank you for your participation. You may now disconnect.
